newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Oilseeds - Millers asked to delay feed rises.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Oilseeds - Millers asked to delay feed rises.

text.p: South Korea's National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (NACF) has asked local feed millers to delay their requests to raise feed prices, but the millers are baulking at any hold up, traders said on Monday.
The NACF said the domestic livestock market, due to be opened from mid-1997, was also suffering from falling prices caused by soft domestic demand.
But feed millers want to increase feed prices in line with strong gains in world soymeal prices and foreign exchange losses, traders said.
"We are expecting domestic feed prices to rise four to five percent from next month," a trader with a major feed milling firm in Korea said.
Traders said several Korean feed millers are expected to buy tapioca, oilseeds and meal this week, traders said.
Two buyer groups, including the Big Feed Mills and the Feed Buying Group, are expected to invite tenders for rapeseed meal, cottonseed meal and wheat bran pellets for shipment from August.
South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) reinvited tenders to buy 50,000 tonnes of tapioca hard pellets and 30,000 tonnes of wheat bran pellets or rice bran pellets on Tuesday.
The NLCF had passed on the tenders last Friday due to high offer prices.
In Japan, traders said they've covered Brazilian soybeans until August shipment, and would buy U.S. origin for July shipment this week after the "Golden Week" holidays.

"Price gains on the Chicago market during the long holidays motivated local end-users to return to the market," a soybean trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said. "The market is quick to react to any bullish news at the moment."
Traders also said some end-users are baulking at buying soybeans until local soymeal prices for the July-September period are fixed.
"It's too early to negotiate local soymeal prices for the third quarter. But the soymeal prices will determine Japan's buying interests later this year," another soybean trader said.
